While Corinne was thus explaining her paintings to Lord Nelvil, she had stopped several times, hoping that he would speak to her; but his wounded soul betrayed itself in no words: only, whenever she expressed a tender idea, he sighed and turned his head away, so that she might not see how easily moved he was in his present state of mind. Corinne, oppressed by this silence, sat down, covering her face with her hands. Lord Nelvil paced briskly about the room for some time; then he approached Corinne and was on the point of voicing his grievance and yielding to what he felt; but a movement of pride, utterly invincible in his character, repressed his tenderness, and he returned to the paintings as though waiting for Corinne to finish showing them to him. She hoped for much from the effect of the last of all; and, making an effort in her turn to appear calm, she rose and said: “Milord, I still have three landscapes left to show you; two allude to certain interesting ideas: I do not much like rural scenes, which are insipid in painting, like idylls, when they make no allusion to Fable or history. What is best, it seems to me, in this genre, is the manner of Salvator Rosa, who represents, as you see in this painting, a rock, torrents, and trees, without a single living being, without even the flight of a bird to recall the idea of life. The absence of man amid nature arouses profound reflections. What would this earth be, thus forsaken? A work without a purpose, and yet a work still so beautiful, whose mysterious impression would be addressed only to the Divinity!

“Finally, here are the two paintings in which, in my opinion, history and poetry are happily united with landscape. One represents the moment when Cincinnatus is invited by the consuls to leave his plough in order to command the Roman armies. It is all the luxuriance of the South that you will see in this landscape: its abundant vegetation, its burning sky, that cheerful air of all nature which is found even in the countenance of the plants. And this other painting, which contrasts with it, is the son of Cairbar asleep upon his father’s tomb. For three days and three nights he has been awaiting the bard who is to pay honors to the memory of the dead. That bard can be seen in the distance, descending the mountain; the father’s shade hovers over the clouds; the countryside is covered with frost; the trees, though stripped bare, are shaken by the winds, and their dead branches and withered leaves still follow the direction of the storm.”

Until then Oswald had continued to feel resentment over what had happened in the garden; but at the sight of this painting, his father’s tomb and the mountains of Scotland rose again in his thoughts, and his eyes filled with tears. Corinne took her harp and, before this painting, began to sing the Scottish ballads whose simple notes seem to accompany the sound of the wind moaning through the valleys. She sang the farewells of a warrior leaving his homeland and his beloved, and Corinne pronounced that word never (_no more_), one of the most harmonious and most affecting in the English language, with the most touching expression. Oswald did not resist the emotion that oppressed him, and both yielded freely to their tears. “Ah!” cried Lord Nelvil, “does that homeland, which is mine, say nothing to thy heart? Wouldst thou follow me into those retreats peopled by my memories? Wouldst thou be the worthy companion of my life, as thou art its charm and enchantment?”—“I believe so,” replied Corinne, “I believe so, since I love you.”—“In the name of love and pity, conceal nothing more from me,” said Oswald.—“You wish it,” Corinne interrupted; “I consent. My promise is given; I attach only one condition to it: that you will not ask me to fulfill it before the approaching time of our religious solemnities. At the moment when I am about to decide my fate, is the support of heaven not more necessary to me than ever?”—“Be assured,” cried Lord Nelvil, “if that fate depends upon me, Corinne, it is no longer in doubt.”—“You believe so,” she resumed; “I do not have the same confidence; but at last, I implore you, show my weakness the indulgence I desire.” Oswald sighed, neither granting nor refusing the requested delay. “Let us leave now,” said Corinne, “and return to the city. How could I conceal anything from you in this solitude! And if what I have to tell you were to estrange you from me, must it be so soon... Let us leave. Oswald, you will return here, whatever may happen; my ashes will rest here.” Oswald, moved and troubled, obeyed Corinne. He returned with her, and during the journey they scarcely spoke to each other. From time to time they looked at one another with an affection that said everything; but nevertheless a feeling of melancholy reigned in the depths of their souls when they reached the heart of Rome.




BOOK NINE

THE POPULAR FESTIVAL AND MUSIC


CHAPTER ONE

It was the day of the noisiest festival of the year, at the end of Carnival, when the Roman people are seized by something like a fever of joy, a frenzy of amusement of which no example is to be found elsewhere. The whole city puts on disguises; scarcely any spectators without masks remain at the windows to watch those who have them; and this gaiety begins on the appointed day at the appointed time, without the public or private events of the year almost ever preventing anyone from enjoying themselves at that season.

It is there that one may judge the full extent of the common people’s imagination. Italian is full of charms, even in their mouths. Alfieri used to say that in Florence he went to the public market to learn good Italian. Rome has the same advantage; and these two cities are perhaps the only ones in the world where the people speak so well that intellectual amusement may be encountered at every street corner.

The kind of gaiety that shines in the authors of harlequinades and comic opera is very commonly found even among uneducated men. During those Carnival days, when exaggeration and caricature are permitted, the most comical scenes take place between the masked revelers.

Often a grotesque gravity contrasts with the Italians’ vivacity, and one would say that their bizarre garments inspire in them a dignity not natural to them. At other times, in the disguises they devise, they display so singular a knowledge of mythology that one would think the ancient fables still popular in Rome. More often, they mock the various ranks of society with a wit full of force and originality. The nation appears a thousand times more distinguished in its games than in its history. The Italian language lends itself to every shade of gaiety with an ease that requires only a slight inflection of the voice, a slightly different ending, to heighten or diminish, ennoble or travesty the meaning of words. It has grace above all in the mouths of children. The innocence of that age and the language’s natural mischievousness form a very piquant contrast. Finally, one might say that it is a language that goes by itself, expresses things without anyone’s intervention, and almost always appears to have more wit than the person who speaks it.
